title: Numbers That Divide Their Positions

concept.title: Start with the most restricted position
body: An arrangement of `1 .. n` is *beautiful* if for every position `i` (counted from 1) the number `v` at position `i` divides `i` or is divisible by `i`: `v % i == 0` or `i % v == 0`. We fill positions with unused numbers and check this rule **at the time of placing**, as in any permutation search with constraints.

Notice the order: the code fills the positions from **`n` down to 1**. A big position such as `n` has very few numbers that fit (only its divisors, and itself), while position 1 accepts anything. Deciding the most restricted positions first makes failures appear early, near the root of the search, where a cut saves the most work. The order in which you fill the positions can change the running time a lot, although the answer is the same.

statement: Count the permutations of `1, 2, ..., n` in which, for every position `i` (from 1 to `n`), the number at position `i` divides `i` or is divisible by `i`.
outputFormat: Print the number of such permutations.
hints: Fill the positions one by one, with unused numbers that satisfy the rule for this position.
Starting from the last position makes the search much faster, because it has the fewest candidates.
Count one when all positions are filled.

explanation: Positions are filled from `n` down to 1 with unused numbers that satisfy the divisibility rule, which cuts most branches early. A completed arrangement counts one.
solution.complexity: Time proportional to the number of partial arrangements (small for n = 15), space O(n).
